old: A Costa Rican 10 colones from 2008, struck in feather-light aluminium. One side carries the national arms: seven stars for the seven provinces, three volcanoes, a sunrise, and the sea on either side for the two oceans Costa Rica sits between. The other side states the value twice over, once in big numerals and once in Braille dots under the word COLONES, so the coin can be read by touch. These aluminium pieces were everyday small change by the hundreds of millions; Costa Rica later switched the denomination to stainless steel to cut costs.

old: A Japanese 10 yen in bronze, dated Heisei 14 (2002), the fourteenth year of Emperor Akihito's reign. One side shows the Phoenix Hall of Byodoin temple in Uji, a thousand-year-old building so loved that it also appears on the 10,000 yen note. The other side frames a big 10 in a wreath of evergreen leaves. Japan has struck this design, nearly unchanged, since 1951, and it is still the 10 yen in everyday pockets today. The collection already holds two Showa-era strikes of the same design from 1982 and 1988; this is its first Heisei one.

old: An Australian 10 cents from 2008, the everyday silver coin with the superb lyrebird fanning its tail across the back — the bird that can mimic almost any sound it hears, drawn here feather by feather. The front carries Queen Elizabeth the Second in Ian Rank-Broadley's portrait, the one Australia used from the late 1990s until the Queen's death. The lyrebird design by Stuart Devlin has been on the 10 cents since decimal currency began in 1966. The collection already holds a 2006 strike of this same coin; this 2008 joins it as a second year.

old: A Mexican one peso from 1975, carrying Jose Maria Morelos, the priest who became a general of Mexico's independence war and was executed for it in 1815. His portrait faces left under the words UN PESO; the other side shows Mexico's national emblem, the eagle with a snake in its beak standing on a cactus — the sign the Aztecs were told to look for when founding their city. Mexico struck this peso, in copper-nickel, through the 1970s and into the early 1980s, and it jingled in every pocket and bus fare in the country. The little Mo beside the portrait is the Mexico City mint's mark, one of the oldest mints in the Americas.

old: Eight doubles from Guernsey, dated 1893 — the oldest coin in this batch, struck while Queen Victoria was on the throne, though Guernsey's coins show no portrait: just the island's shield with its three lions, inherited from the island's Norman past, and a sprig of leaves. The double was Guernsey's own money, a Channel Islands coinage counted eight to a British penny, and this big bronze piece is the penny-sized one — Guernsey kept its doubles for a century before joining the pound in full. It is the collection's first coin from Guernsey. This one has lived a life: dark, worn smooth in places, with pale corrosion spots on the shield side.
